sentences.text: The genus Nemegtomaia was formally described by Lü and colleagues in the year 2005.
Nemegtomaia possessed a well-developed crest formed primarily by the premaxilla bones of its snout.
This animal is estimated to have been around 2 meters in length and weighed 40 kilograms.
The shoulder blade of Nemegtomaia appears to have been 185 mm or 7 inches in total length.
A fossil of Nemegtomaia was discovered in a brooding posture over a nest containing eggs.
The fossilized nest associated with the Nemegtomaia specimen measures approximately 90 cm wide and 100 cm long.
The fossil specimen of Nemegtomaia was preserved in sediment deposited by a sandstorm or dune shift.
Evidence of borings and burrows in the Nemegtomaia fossil indicates it was scavenged by colonies of skin beetles and possibly other insects.
Yoshitsugu Kobayashi discovered an incomplete oviraptorid skeleton in the Nemegt Formation of the Gobi Desert in 1996.
The first specimen of Nemegtomaia was discovered in 1996 and formally named in 2004.
The first new specimen was found less than 500 meters from the holotype and was assigned to Nemegtomaia based on similar anatomy and location.
The nesting specimen was positioned on top of what was likely a ring of eggs, with its arms crossed over them.
Seven distinct eggs and fragments were found within the nest, some located beneath the skeleton's skull and limbs.
The eggs associated with the nesting specimen were estimated to be 5 to 6 cm wide and 14 to 16 cm long when intact.
Research in 2010 suggested that the jaws of oviraptorids, including Nemegtomaia, shared structural similarities with herbivorous animals like dicynodonts.
In 2017, researchers proposed that the parrot-like jaws of oviraptorids might indicate a diet including fruits, nuts, and seeds.
Evidence suggests Nemegtomaia preferred to nest near streams to access soft, sandy substrate and food.
In 2026, Chun-Yu Su and colleagues conducted an experiment to test if oviraptorids used body heat for incubation.
Experiments showed that oviraptorid brooding would result in uneven temperatures and lower incubation efficiency compared to modern birds.
Researchers concluded that oviraptorids likely co-regulated incubation using environmental and solar heat rather than body heat alone.
A 2015 study found it unlikely that Nemegtomaia possessed bird-like skull mobility because the quadrate bone was immobile.
In 2010, Longrich and colleagues classified Nemegtomaia in the family Oviraptoridae and subfamily Ingeniinae, noting it was the only member of that subfamily with a prominent crest.
In 2010, researchers classified Nemegtomaia as a member of the Oviraptoridae family within the subfamily Ingeniinae.
The subfamily name Ingeniinae was replaced by Heyuanninae because the name Ingenia was already occupied.
Nemegtomaia lived in what is now Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 70 million years ago.
Nemegtomaia lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the upper Campanian to lower Maastrichtian ages.
The family Oviraptoridae, to which Nemegtomaia belongs, is exclusively known from the Upper Cretaceous of Asia, with most genera found in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia and China.
The rivers of the Nemegt Formation supported diverse aquatic life including molluscs, fish, turtles, and the crocodylomorph Shamosuchus.
The Nemegt Formation contained herbivorous dinosaurs such as the ankylosaurid Tarchia, the pachycephalosaur Prenocephale, hadrosaurs like Saurolophus, and sauropods like Nemegtosaurus.
Gregory S. Paul suggested in 2010 that crestless oviraptorids were juveniles or females of crested species, implying the number of genera in the group was exaggerated.
Other researchers argue that dromaeosaurs and troodontids are most closely related to birds, placing oviraptorosaurs outside this group.
